corpus.source: NuGet top-100 by downloads (azuresearch), fetched 2026-08-06, resolved through each package's nuspec SourceLink <repository url + commit> to a GitHub source archive at that exact commit; .cs files
corpus.source_note: NuGet ships compiled assemblies, not source — there is not one .cs file in any of the top 20 packages — so unlike the crates.io/npm/Maven corpora this one is repository source, tests and samples and build tooling included, at the commit the package was built from. Of the top 100: 50 fetched, 13 skipped because a higher-ranked package already claimed the same repo+commit, 8 with no usable nuspec repository metadata, the rest for other resolve failures. The result is dominated by two Microsoft monorepos (dotnet/dotnet, Azure/azure-sdk-for-net), so file counts here reflect repository size, not package popularity.
corpus.remaining_gaps_note: Of the 7,148 files the oracle calls valid and the grammar rejects, 5,040 contain #if/#elif/#else/#endif. Reducing each of those to the configuration Roslyn actually parsed (no preprocessor symbols defined, so every #if is false and only #else survives) and re-parsing shows 4,617 of them parse cleanly — they fail only because the grammar parses branches the oracle never saw. That class is inherent, not a fixable grammar bug: a file whose #if and #else each supply half a namespace declaration, or half a parameter list, has no single well-formed tree. The actionable queue is the other 2,531 files: 2,108 with no conditional compilation at all, plus the 423 that still fail after reduction.
corpus.oracle: tools/cs-oracle — Roslyn's own parser (CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText) at LanguageVersion.Latest, the newest stable C#, not Preview. Parse-only, so unresolved types are not errors and each file is judged on its own. Requires the .NET SDK; it is built on first use.

patches.title: `async` is a contextual keyword, not a reserved word
patches.origin: local; found by NuGet top-100 sweep

evidence.repro: Run(async); Run(async: true); var resultCode = async;
evidence.spec: `async` is contextual in C#: it modifies a method, lambda or anonymous method, but is a legal identifier everywhere else. It joins the grammar's existing _reserved_identifier list next to `var`, `when`, `where` and `yield`, at prec(-2) so the modifier and lambda readings still win wherever they apply — a plain conflict declaration was not enough, because a bare `async` can start a method modifier, a lambda modifier or an identifier and the ambiguity reappears inside every declaration-list repeat.
